introduction.p: The last section brought conics into one family. A parabola, ellipse, or hyperbola can be described by one polar equation:
The number e decides the type of curve. When 0<e<1, the curve is an ellipse.
This is not only a classification trick. It is the equation that appears in one of the great discoveries of science: planets move on ellipses with the sun at a focus.

That sentence is Kepler’s first law. We use the ideal two-body model: the central body is fixed, the force is inverse-square attraction, and other bodies and drag are neglected. It belongs naturally here because the focus of a polar conic sits at the pole.

statement.p: A centered Cartesian ellipse puts the origin at the geometric center. Kepler’s first law puts the sun at a focus. In your own words, why are polar coordinates better suited to that geometry?

subsection.title: Kepler’s second law as swept area
subsection.p: Kepler’s first law says that a planet moves on an ellipse with the sun at one focus.
Kepler’s second law says something about the speed of the motion.

note.title: Kepler’s second law
note.p: The line segment from the sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.

subsection.p: This is an area statement, so it should remind us of the polar area formula:

Equivalently,
This equation has a simple geometric meaning. When the planet is close to the sun, r is small. To keep
constant, the angular speed \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} must be larger. When the planet is far from the sun, r is large, so the angular speed is smaller.

p.me: \text{Planets move faster near the sun and slower far from the sun.}

subsection.p: The equal-area law directly controls angular speed. To check the ordinary speed along this elliptical orbit, write h=r^2\theta'>0. From r=p/(1+e\cos\theta), differentiation gives r'=he\sin\theta/p. Hence v^2=(r')^2+(r\theta')^2=(h/p)^2(1+e^2+2e\cos\theta)=(h/p)^2(e^2-1+2p/r). This increases as the distance r decreases, so the speed is also larger nearer the sun.

exercise.title: What does Kepler’s second law say in the language of polar area?

statement.p: Equal areas in equal times means the swept-area rate dA/dt is constant. In your own words, why does the polar area element dA=\frac12 r^2\,d\theta turn that statement into a fact about r^2\theta', and why must a planet move faster when it is closer to the sun?

hint.p: If \frac12 r^2\theta' is constant, a smaller r forces a larger angular speed. The same ellipse is traced at different speeds.

subsection.title: Central force preview
subsection.p: Kepler discovered his laws from astronomical data. Newton explained them from a force law.
The key idea is that gravity is a central force. It points along the line from the planet to the sun.
Gravity pulls the planet inward along the radial direction; it has no sideways force component.
This sideways fact is what produces equal areas in equal times.

exercise.title: Why does a central force produce equal areas in equal times?

statement.p: A central gravitational force has no tangential component. Explain why this implies conservation of r^2\theta\prime and which additional coordinate calculations are needed for a full orbit derivation.

hint.p: No sideways force means the areal velocity does not change. Single-variable calculus can compute swept area; explaining the force as a vector is the next subject.

note.title: What we have seen
note.p: Single-variable calculus can describe the orbit as a polar curve and compute swept area.
Multivariable calculus explains why the motion follows that curve.

subsection.p: The bridge is already visible. A planet is a moving point, like the parametric curves at the start of this chapter. Its coordinates change with time. Its velocity and acceleration are pairs of derivatives. Its force has a direction.
So the chapter’s first idea returns in a richer form:

p.me: \text{a curve is not only a set of points; it can be a motion.}

subsection.p: The next optional bridge uses the same plane in a different language. Instead of writing a point as (x,y), or as (r,\theta), we write it as one number:
That number is complex, and multiplication by it knows about rotation.

exercise.title: What is the difference between the orbit shape and the motion along it?

statement.p: The polar equation r=p/(1+e\cos\theta) describes the curve. Kepler’s second law describes how the planet travels that curve. In your own words, why is that the same distinction as a geometric curve versus a parametrization?

hint.p: The set of points is the orbit. The schedule along those points is the motion. Area-sweeping is information about the schedule.
